344.title: Sleep: the bird returns to the tree (6.8)
344.hook: a bird on a string flies every way, finds no rest, and comes back to where it's tied; so does the mind, every night
344.howItsDone: Many Hindu teachers use Uddalaka's tethered bird as an image for meditation on the breath, and the Upanishads' study of sleep, dream and deep sleep became a central theme in Vedanta.

segments.voice: Yesterday: food, and the ember and the straw. The finest part of food becomes mind. Your line was you are what you eat, literally. Week three of year two begins.
screen: `FOOD — YOU ARE WHAT YOU EAT, LITERALLY.`

segments.voice: Some nights your mind will not land. It's 1am and it's flying through tomorrow's meeting, last week's argument, a thing you said in seventh grade. Every direction, nowhere to rest. And then, at some point you never notice, it stops. You wake up and it's morning. Where did you go? Uddalaka has an answer, and it starts with a pun.
screen: `1AM, AND THE MIND WON'T LAND.` → `THEN, SOMEHOW, IT STOPS.` → `WHERE DID YOU GO?`

segments.voice: Learn from me about sleep, my dear, Uddalaka says. When a person sleeps, they become one with Being. They have gone to their own. He's playing on the Sanskrit. The word for he sleeps is svapiti. Uddalaka hears in it svam apita: gone to one's own. Sleep is going home. Then the picture. A bird tied by a string flies off this way, and that way, and every way, looking for somewhere else to rest, and finds nowhere. So in the end it settles down at the very place it's tied. The mind, he says, is just like that. It flies in every direction, finds no rest anywhere else, and settles down in the breath. For the mind, my dear, is tied to the breath. Think about that at 1am. All that flying is the bird pulling at the string, looking for rest out there, in plans and replays. Rest is coming back to where you're tied: the breath, and beneath the breath, the Upanishad says, Being itself. Then, at the end of this lesson, Uddalaka says for the very first time the three words he'll keep repeating to his son: tat tvam asi. You are that. A handful of salt will open them properly in a few days. For now, notice where the father chose to say them first: in a lesson about sleep. Every night, without trying, you go home.

segments.voice: Let the mind fly wherever it wants for a few breaths, plans, worries, memories, and just watch it pull at the string. Then notice the breath, where the string is tied, and each time the mind flies off, let it land again on the next breath out.
Sleep. In Uddalaka's teaching, going to one's own: the mind, like a tethered bird, comes to rest in the breath and in Being.
Your line: rest is return. Tomorrow, the bees and the honey they make. Sleep well.

345.title: The bees and the honey — no juice says "I am from this tree" (6.9)
345.hook: bees gather nectar from many different trees, and in the honey, no drop can say which tree it came from
345.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers often take Uddalaka's lessons one at a time, as here, and the honey image is one of several the Chandogya uses for creatures merging into Being in sleep and death.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sleep, the bird on a string coming back to where it's tied. Your line was rest is return.

Pick up a jar of honey. Wildflower, the label says. Bees visited clover, dandelion, an apple tree, a lime tree, and plenty of flowers no one will ever list. They brought it all home and worked it together into one golden thing. Try to find the apple-tree part. You can't. It's not gone; it's in there. It just can't be picked out anymore. Uddalaka, teaching his son, picks up the same jar.
screen: `WILDFLOWER HONEY.` → `CLOVER, DANDELION, APPLE, LIME.` → `FIND THE APPLE-TREE PART.`

segments.voice: Just as bees make honey, my dear, Uddalaka says, by gathering the juices of many different trees and bringing them to a single sweetness, and in the honey those juices can't tell one another, I am the juice of this tree, I am the juice of that tree, in the same way all these creatures, when they merge into Being, in deep sleep and at death, don't know: we have merged into Being. Then a line that's easy to skip, and shouldn't be. Whatever they are in this world, a tiger, a lion, a wolf, a boar, a worm, a moth, a gnat, a mosquito, they become that again. So the honey isn't the end of the story. Hold both halves. In the depth of Being, the separate names are gone. And here, in the world, the tiger wakes up a tiger and the mosquito a mosquito. Uddalaka isn't erasing anyone's life. In his picture, underneath a name, a family, a whole history, there's one sweetness shared with everything that lives. And from the inside, no one notices the merging. A person sleeps, wakes up, and goes back to being themselves. Then, once again, the refrain: that subtle essence is the self of all this; that is the truth; that is the self; you are that, Shvetaketu. Please, sir, says the son, tell me more.

346.title: The rivers and the sea (6.10)
346.hook: rivers run east and west, each with its own name, and in the sea not one of them can say 'I am this river'
346.tomorrow: the tree: cut it, it bleeds
346.howItsDone: Rivers are sacred for many Hindus, who bathe in them on festival days and immerse ashes after cremation; Vedanta teachers often use Uddalaka's rivers and the sea to describe the relation of the self to Brahman.

segments.voice: Yesterday: madhu, many juices, one sweetness. Your line was the rivers lose their names, and today, here are those rivers.

Rivers have names, and people love those names. They write songs about them, fight over them, scatter ashes in them, bathe in them on holy days. The Ganga, the Yamuna, the Mississippi, the Thames. A river has a source, a path, a personality: slow and brown, or fast and cold. Then it reaches the sea. Stand on a beach and look out. Which part of that water was the Ganga? Uddalaka asks his son the same thing.
screen: `RIVERS HAVE NAMES.` → `SONGS, ASHES, HOLY DAYS.` → `WHICH PART WAS THE GANGA?`

segments.voice: These rivers, my dear, Uddalaka says, the eastern ones flow toward the east, the western ones toward the west. They go from sea to sea. They become the sea itself. And there, in the sea, they don't know: I am this river, I am that one. Notice that little phrase, from sea to sea. Commentators hear the water cycle in it: water rises from the sea as cloud, falls as rain, gathers into rivers, and runs back home. The river was the sea all along, on a long walk. Then he turns it around. In the same way, my dear, all these creatures, though they have come from Being, don't know: we have come from Being. Yesterday's honey was about going in and losing the label. Today is about coming out and forgetting the source. A river in the mountains doesn't feel like the ocean. It feels narrow, rushing, very much itself. A person can feel like that too: a particular someone, with particular worries. And Uddalaka says again, whatever they are here, tiger or lion or gnat, they become that. The river is truly a river while it runs. He only points out where it comes from and where it goes. Then the refrain once more: that subtle essence is the self of all this world; you are that, Shvetaketu. Some Vedanta schools hear the river as finally nothing but sea. Others hear it as a real, beloved part of the sea.

347.title: The tree — cut it, it bleeds; leave it, it lives (6.11)
347.hook: strike a great tree at the root and sap runs out, but it lives; when life leaves a branch, the branch dries up
347.howItsDone: At Hindu deathbeds and funerals, families may recite or reflect on scriptures that teach that the self does not die with the body, from the Upanishads to the Bhagavad Gita's second chapter.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samudra, rivers that run from sea to sea and forget their names. Your line was the sea.

Find an old tree with a scar: where a branch was cut, or a car hit it, or someone carved initials years ago. Often you'll see where the sap ran, dried now into a hard, shiny crust. The tree bled. And it's still standing, still leafing out every spring. Next to it, maybe, one branch is gray and bare, and never came back. Same tree. One part alive, one part not. Uddalaka points his son to a great tree.
screen: `AN OLD TREE WITH A SCAR.` → `IT BLED, AND IT'S STILL STANDING.` → `ONE GRAY BRANCH.`

segments.voice: If someone were to strike this great tree at its root, my dear, Uddalaka says, it would bleed sap, but it would live. Strike it in the middle, it would bleed, but live. Strike it at the top, it would bleed, but live. Filled through and through by the living self, the jiva atman, it stands, drinking in water, rejoicing. But if life leaves one branch, that branch dries up. If it leaves a second, or a third, they dry up. If it leaves the whole tree, the whole tree dries up. Then the line that turns it toward his son. In the same way, my dear, understand this: the body dies when life leaves it. But life does not die. Look at the order. First, life is everywhere in the tree: root, middle, top. You can wound it anywhere and it carries on, because life isn't sitting in one spot you could cut out. It pervades. Second, the body depends on life, not the other way around. A dry branch isn't the death of life; it's life leaving that branch. For Uddalaka, the same is true of a person. The body is a tree. Something fills it, makes it drink and grow and rejoice, and when that something leaves, the body falls. But what left doesn't fall with it. And once again, the refrain: you are that, Shvetaketu.

segments.voice: Bring your attention to your feet, your roots, and feel something alive there: warmth, tingling, a pulse. Move up through your belly and chest, where the breath moves, to your face and scalp, the same life from root to crown, and rest in it the way the tree stands, drinking in water.
The tree. Uddalaka's great tree, filled by the living self: wounded, it lives; when life leaves, it dries; the body dies, but life does not.

348.title: The banyan seed — "break it. what do you see? nothing. from that nothing, this tree"…
348.hook: the father has his son split a banyan fig, then a seed inside it, and asks what he sees: nothing at all
348.howItsDone: The banyan is sacred to many Hindus and is often worshipped, especially by women during the Vat Savitri festival; teachers use Uddalaka's banyan seed to explain the subtle essence behind the visible world.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the tree, struck at root, middle and top, bleeding but alive. Your line was life pervades.

A banyan doesn't stop at one trunk. It sends roots down from its branches, and those roots thicken into new trunks, until one tree can look like a small forest. Birds nest in it, people sit in its shade, and all of it is one tree. Its fruit is a little fig a bird could swallow whole, with seeds like specks of dust inside. Uddalaka sends his son to fetch one.
screen: `A TREE THAT LOOKS LIKE A FOREST.` → `ROOTS THAT BECOME TRUNKS.` → `IT STARTED AS A TINY SEED.`

segments.voice: The lesson is a short conversation, almost a game. Bring me a fruit from that banyan. Here it is, sir. Break it. It's broken, sir. What do you see? These tiny seeds, sir. Break one of them. It's broken, sir. What do you see there? Nothing at all, sir. And the father says: my dear, that subtle essence you can't see, from that very essence this great banyan tree stands. Believe me, my dear. He doesn't describe the seed. He has his son break it with his own hands and look, and the son reports honestly: nothing. That nothing is the point. Not empty nothing. Too-fine-to-see nothing. Uddalaka's word is anima, the subtlest, the finest. The whole enormous tree, trunks and roots and shade and birds, rests on something so fine it can't be seen at all. Then he asks for something he hasn't asked before: shraddhatsva, believe me, have faith. Not belief instead of looking; his son has just looked as hard as anyone can. One way to hear it: at the edge of what can be seen, don't conclude there's nothing there. The tree is standing right in front of you. Then the refrain: that subtle essence is the self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the self. You are that, Shvetaketu.

349.title: The salt in water — "taste it here. here. everywhere." (6.13)
349.hook: drop salt in water overnight; in the morning you can't find it, but sip from any side and it's there
349.howItsDone: Tat tvam asi is one of the four mahavakyas, the great sayings, and in some traditions it is taught to monks at their initiation; each Vedanta school has its own commentary on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anima, the seed broken open, and nothing at all inside. Your line was the subtle essence.

Take a glass of water and a pinch of salt. Drop the salt in, and watch the grains sink, cloud and disappear. Leave it overnight. In the morning, try to pick the salt back out. You can't. It isn't anywhere you can point to. And yet you know it's in there, and you know exactly how to find out. This is Uddalaka's most famous lesson, where his three-word refrain lands with full weight.
screen: `A GLASS OF WATER, A PINCH OF SALT.` → `IN THE MORNING, PICK IT OUT.` → `YOU CAN'T. BUT IT'S THERE.`

segments.voice: Put this salt in water, Uddalaka says, and come to me in the morning. Shvetaketu does. In the morning his father says: bring me the salt you put in last night. He looks, and can't find it; it has dissolved. Sip from this end. How is it? Salty. From the middle? Salty. From the far end? Salty. Then, the father says, you don't see Being here, my dear, but it is truly here. That subtle essence is the self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the self. Tat tvam asi, Shvetaketu. You are that. Those three words are among the most famous in Hindu scripture. Tat, that. Tvam, you. Asi, are. Later teachers counted them among the four great sayings, the mahavakyas, of the Upanishads. The honey and the rivers showed the names dissolving. The seed showed the essence too fine to see. The salt shows it's everywhere at once, in every sip, every drop. And the schools of Vedanta hear the three words differently. Shankara's Advaita hears pure identity: your deepest self and Being are one. Ramanuja hears the self as real and distinct, yet belonging to Brahman, the way a body belongs to its soul. Madhva's Dvaita school reads the same Sanskrit with a different word break, as atat tvam asi: you are not that, not the same as the Lord. Each school has a long line of teachers behind it. 350.title: The blindfolded man led home (6.14)
350.hook: a man is led away blindfolded and left in the wilderness; someone unties him and points, and he asks his way home, village by village
350.tomorrow: the dying man and the fire ordeal
350.howItsDone: Hindu traditions give the guru, the teacher, a place of honor, and many communities observe Guru Purnima each year to give thanks to their teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Being, unseen yet truly here, like salt in water. Your line was salty, salty, salty. Today ends week three of year two.

Honey and rivers, trees and seeds and salt. And still, maybe, Shvetaketu is thinking what anyone would think. Fine. Being is everywhere, and I am that. So why don't I feel it? Why am I still lost? His father doesn't scold him, and doesn't repeat the salt one more time. He tells him about a man led far from home with a cloth tied over his eyes.
screen: `HONEY, RIVERS, TREES, SEEDS, SALT.` → `SO WHY DON'T I FEEL IT?` → `A MAN WITH A CLOTH OVER HIS EYES.`

segments.voice: Suppose, Uddalaka says, someone leads a man away from his home in Gandhara with his eyes covered, and leaves him in a lonely, empty place. The man turns and shouts, east, north, south: I was brought here blindfolded and left here blindfolded! Then someone unties the cloth and says: Gandhara is that way. Go. And the man, asking from village to village, informed and thinking for himself, gets all the way home. In the same way, Uddalaka says, a person who has a teacher knows. Look at who does what. The stranger doesn't carry the man home. He takes off the blindfold and points. The man still has to walk, and ask, and use his own head. A teacher, in this picture, isn't a taxi. A teacher points. And the man didn't lack legs or a road. Gandhara was there the whole time; he just couldn't see which way to turn. Uddalaka adds that for such a person, the only delay is until he's released from the body; then he arrives. And the refrain: you are that, Shvetaketu. This week, in order: sleep, the bird coming back to where it's tied. The honey, where no juice knows its tree. The rivers and the sea. The tree that bleeds and lives. Anima, and nothing inside. Being in the salt. And today, the blindfold untied.
